title: Freya and the Summer
premise: Ines Amberdale, a cellist whose career ended in a humiliating collapse at her final conservatory performance, has retreated to a small coastal town where she repairs instruments and keeps her heart as carefully archived as her old scores. When a letter postmarked eleven years ago falls out of a donated violin case — written by her first love, Freya, who vanished without explanation the summer they turned nineteen — Ines is forced to confront not just what was lost, but why. As she searches for Freya, now living under a changed name and hiding from a wrongful conviction that destroyed both their families, Ines must choose between the safe, fragmentary life she has built and the whole-hearted risk of love, testimony, and truth. The novel ends with Freya's name cleared through evidence Ines uncovers in the letter's original envelope, and with the two of them performing together — Ines on cello, Freya on violin — on the last night before the bakery below Ines's apartment closes its lease for good.
about_author: August Voss is the pen name of a former orchestral librarian who spent a decade cataloguing other people's music before writing their own stories. They live near the sea and believe every unfinished letter deserves an ending.

chapters.title: The Tuning Silence
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Three years after her catastrophic final performance, Ines repairs instruments in a coastal town and avoids playing altogether. A bakery lease notice arrives for her building, threatening her fragile routine. The emotional beat is quiet dread: a life built to avoid risk is already cracking.

chapters.title: What the Violin Case Kept
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. A donation box brings in a battered violin; inside the lining, Ines finds a yellowed letter addressed to her, postmarked eleven years ago, in Freya's unmistakable handwriting. She cannot bring herself to open it. The beat is vertigo — the past arriving with a date stamp.

chapters.title: Eleven Summers Ago
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, interwoven flashback. The summer of the letter: two teenagers, a boathouse, first love, and Freya's family scandal breaking like weather. The chapter establishes what was lost and how completely Ines sealed it away. Beat: tenderness shadowed by approaching ruin.

chapters.title: Unopened
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines carries the letter for days, opening it finally at midnight: Freya writes of being framed for embezzlement at her father's firm and of running rather than destroying Ines's future by association. The last line: 'If you ever read this, don't look for me.' Beat: grief rekindled into resolve.

chapters.title: Don't Look For Me
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Of course she looks. She pulls old newspaper archives and learns Freya was convicted, served four years, and disappeared after release under suspicion of fleeing probation. Beat: the romance plot braids into the justice plot; Ines realizes loving Freya means believing her.

chapters.title: The Bakery Downstairs
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Her landlord, Marta, reveals the building sold; the bakery closing means Ines loses her workshop too. But Marta remembers a quiet woman who bought bread here two winters ago — paid cash, flinched from cameras. Beat: hope disguised as coincidence.

chapters.title: A Woman Who Buys Bread
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Following Marta's thread, Ines traces a woman named 'June Hallow' working at a garden nursery two towns over. She watches from across the road and knows the way June ties back her hair. Beat: longing sharpened into fear of what reunion might cost them both.

chapters.title: June
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, first time. Freya has built a careful, small life under a false name — until she sees Ines standing among the rose bushes and everything she buried floods back. She sends Ines away. Beat: terror masquerading as coldness; we learn Freya believes someone is still watching her.

chapters.title: The Man From the Firm
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Flashback and present: the real thief was her father's business partner, Aldous Crane, who framed her when she found discrepancies. He has recently been promoted, honored, untouchable — and Freya spotted his car outside her nursery last week. Beat: paranoia confirmed; stakes escalate.

chapters.title: Second Movement
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Refusing to be sent away, Ines leaves her card and, impulsively, plays cello outside the nursery at closing time — her first public playing since the collapse. It's rough, trembling, alive. June doesn't come out, but the next morning there's bread on Ines's step. Beat: music as a language neither can deny.

chapters.title: Terms of Contact
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. They meet on neutral ground — a cliff path — and negotiate like diplomats: no police, no press, no promises. Ines offers help finding proof of Crane's fraud; Freya offers nothing but the truth of eleven years ago. Beat: wary reconnection, old intimacy flickering under new armor.

chapters.title: Ledgers and Lies
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Research montage: Ines uses her instrument-repair network to reach a retired firm accountant, Mrs. Okonkwo, who kept copies of records Crane thought destroyed. The numbers show Crane siphoned funds and pinned it on Freya's father, who died disgraced. Beat: righteous anger; justice taking shape outside the law.

chapters.title: What Ines Broke
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya confronts Ines about the night of Ines's failed concert — revealing she was in the audience, having come back secretly to see her play, and fled when she saw reporters covering the Crane case nearby. Ines's collapse and Freya's disappearance were entangled all along. Beat: devastating mutual reckoning; guilt exchanged like contraband.

chapters.title: Crane Notices
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Crane's investigator photographs Ines visiting Mrs. Okonkwo. Crane, feeling the past stir, applies pressure: an anonymous complaint gets Freya reported to authorities under her old identity. Beat: the clock starts — Freya may be arrested within weeks unless the truth lands first.

chapters.title: Lending Pieces
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines proposes going public — a journalist, an exposé — but Freya refuses, terrified of trial, of Ines becoming collateral. They fight. Ines accuses Freya of still deciding for both of them, the way she did at nineteen. Beat: the central romantic wound opened: protection versus partnership.

chapters.title: The Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Alone, Freya takes out the donated violin — the one Ines repaired and quietly left for her — and plays for the first time in eleven years. She reads Ines's old letters, kept all this time, and understands Ines never stopped choosing her. Beat: surrender beginning; the heart arguing past the fear.

chapters.title: Okonkwo's Condition
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Mrs. Okonkwo agrees to testify or provide documents publicly — but only if Freya consents to reclaim her real name, because justice requires a person, not a ghost. Ines must deliver this ultimatum to the woman she loves. Beat: the theme crystallized — identity cannot be healed while hidden.

chapters.title: Freya Again
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya signs her true name for the first time in a decade — on a sworn statement Okonkwo's documents will anchor. That night she and Ines stop negotiating and finally speak plainly, then touch like people resuming a sentence interrupted mid-word. Beat: climax of the emotional arc; whole heart, no pieces lent.

chapters.title: Crane Moves First
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Crane, tipped off, breaks into the workshop seeking the documents; Ines, hiding them, confronts him alone and records his threats on her phone — including an admission he falsified the ledgers. Freya arrives; together they hold him until police come, Freya using her real name openly for the first time. Beat: external climax; danger faced side by side.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The fallout: Crane arrested, the conviction petition reopened, Freya's father's name posthumously cleared. Freya gives her statement without flinching. Ines waits outside the courthouse and plays Bach on the steps — unafraid now of audiences. Beat: justice achieved outside and then inside the law; exorcism complete.

chapters.title: Last Night of the Lease
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The bakery closes; Marta throws a farewell evening. Ines and Freya perform a duet in the empty shop — cello and violin, the piece they never finished at nineteen — while neighbors fill the room. Beat: resolution of the performance trauma; love performed in public, finally.

chapters.title: New Postmark
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, closing chapter. Months later: charges formally dropped, a new lease signed jointly above the reopened bakery-workshop, and a fresh letter — this one delivered by hand, beginning 'Dear Ines' and continuing for pages about the future instead of the past. Final line mirrors the old one: 'Look for me. I'm right here.' Beat: memory integrated, identity claimed, love in present tense.
